It knows, on the one hand, what the successive stages or types are, and on the other, why they succeed one another in precisely this order.
First, this allows Phenomenology to divide history correctly into periods—to identify the moment when a genuinely new historical stage emerges.
The duration of these stages—the time between the emergence of historical type A and the emergence of type B that follows it—can vary enormously, from a few years to several centuries.
But Phenomenology will treat each stage as a single whole. More exactly, it will select from each stage its most typical and defining element.

For this reason, the phenomenological or dialectical description of history can at first look astonishingly arbitrary. Phenomenology leaves out vast numbers of “historical facts” and seems simply to “jump” from one historical situation to another.
But once its method is understood, we see that these omissions and jumps are grounded in the dialectic itself.

Second, dialectical knowledge of the “causes” and “effects” belonging to each stage allows Phenomenology to describe only what is genuinely new at that stage and what is already quietly preparing the next one.

Phenomenology therefore not only leaves out most “historical facts.” It also reduces the facts it does discuss to an extreme schematic form, producing what looks, from the historian’s point of view, like a very incomplete picture.
But this “schematization” is justified in several ways, which will become clear from the text of the Phenomenology itself.
Finally, knowing the “essence” of these stages or types of conscious existence allows Phenomenology to idealize historical facts.
A type of conscious existence described by Phenomenology—the “slave,” the “skeptic,” the “bourgeois,” and so on—may never have existed anywhere in what we might call a chemically pure form.

It is entirely possible that no flesh-and-blood human being ever lived completely in the way demanded by a particular type of existence, or ever understood that form of existence as fully as it could have been understood.

In this respect—and, strictly speaking, always—the phenomenologist “invents” a person who perfectly and completely embodies the type in question, usually by combining different traits found among people of the same historical period.
To the scholarly historian, phenomenological “history” may therefore look not merely fragmentary and schematic but positively arbitrary and “fantastical.”

But once the historian has understood, through Phenomenology, the dialectical law governing the development of human existence, he will also understand the necessity and legitimacy not only of its periodization and schematization of history, but also of its idealization of historical forms.
We can end our preliminary account of the object and subject matter of Phenomenology here.

Before moving on, however, I want to emphasize once again—or revisit—the fact that Phenomenology, insofar as it is a “dialectical anthropology,” also appears as the phenomenologist’s own “dialectical autobiography.”
In other words, it is an autobiography of its own author.

We have seen that the phenomenologist must necessarily end his Phenomenology by describing his own self-consciousness—that is, by giving a true description of himself, insofar as his self-consciousness really is complete and his Phenomenology really is “finished.”
This necessity follows from the very purpose of Phenomenology.
Phenomenology is supposed to make philosophy genuinely possible. It must therefore make its author—and its reader—into a philosopher.
But the philosopher is precisely the human being who possesses complete knowledge of himself: knowledge that fully exhausts his self-consciousness.
Phenomenology must therefore end with the emergence of its author’s own complete self-consciousness.
The same conclusion follows from the nature of its object and subject matter.
If Phenomenology describes all appearances, it must also describe itself as an “appearance.”

And if the description of any appearance must be completed by a description of the corresponding cognition and consciousness, then the phenomenologist must also describe himself, insofar as his consciousness contains the experience whose content is the Phenomenology he has written.
Phenomenology therefore necessarily contains the self-consciousness of its own author.
But this self-consciousness appears within Phenomenology as the result of the entire historical development described before it.
That development thereby becomes, so to speak, the history of this self-consciousness, and the whole of Phenomenology becomes an auto-biography: the account of the history of a life.

Yet the “history” in question consists of the stages in the development of one human being’s self-consciousness, as described by Phenomenology—or the stages of that human being’s appearance to himself—rather than the historical development of the flesh-and-blood individual as such.
Phenomenology therefore gives us the “history” of the phenomenologist’s consciousness, not the biography of the phenomenologist as a concrete biological individual.
Its “autobiography” is not an autobiography in the ordinary sense. It is a philosophical, or more exactly phenomenological, autobiography.
It describes its author only insofar as he is its author, leaving aside everything in his life that belongs merely to him as an ordinary person.
Taken as a whole—at its end—the Phenomenology allows its author, if one wishes, to answer completely the philosophical question about himself:
“Who am I, and why am I doing what I am doing?”

But that answer can be complete only if I do not consider myself simply as a living individual—I, Alexandre Vladimirovich Kojevnikov—but instead as an “anonymous” phenomenologist and future philosopher.
That is, I must reduce my relevant activity to the writing of the Phenomenology in preparation for writing a philosophical system.
At that point the philosophical problem becomes a phenomenological one, and I can answer it completely.
I am the person writing—or who has written—this Phenomenology.
What am I doing—or what have I done?
I am writing—or have written—this Phenomenology.
Read the whole thing and you will see. Only the Phenomenology itself can answer that question.
Why am I writing it—or why did I write it?
Because I hoped that through it I could become a philosopher.
That too is explained in the Phenomenology itself, especially in its “Introduction.”
But why did I hope that writing the Phenomenology could make me a philosopher?
The Phenomenology itself answers this question, but I can already give the answer in a few words.
My Phenomenology—or, more exactly, Hegel’s Phenomenology, which I first read and which is incorporated into my own—shows me, first:
that concrete or philosophical knowledge—that is, perfect knowledge or omniscience—is in principle possible, but must be preceded by phenomenological knowledge;
that such knowledge has not yet actually been achieved, not even by Hegel;
that Hegel’s philosophy has come closer to it than anything else;

that after the appearance of Hegel’s philosophy, and in connection with it, Marx, Lenin, and Stalin created new historical conditions—that is, a new type of conscious human existence, specifically a socialist type—which both requires and makes possible a critical revision and extension of Hegel’s philosophy, together with the Phenomenology contained within it;

and finally, that according to my own Phenomenology, nothing produced since Hegel can yet be regarded as this corrected and completed philosophy suited to the new historical conditions, or as a Phenomenology corresponding to such a philosophy.
So this philosophy is possible, but it does not yet exist.
That is precisely why I can hope to create it.
But why is it specifically I who hopes to do so?
Here it is easy to see that the Phenomenology cannot provide an answer.
The fact that I am its author will become known only when—and because—I have actually written a Philosophy.
Phenomenology can, however, state the conditions that any author of a Phenomenology must satisfy.
Such a person must write—or think through—a Phenomenology that essentially coincides with the one I am writing or have written.

This means a Phenomenology that, on the one hand, incorporates everything in Hegel’s Phenomenology that has passed the test of dialectical verification through the historical development that continued after Hegel, and that, on the other hand, gives an additional and correct phenomenological account of that later development.

All of this means that I can hope to become a philosopher and go beyond Hegel’s philosophy only if I possess phenomenological knowledge of everything that has happened on Earth up to and including Hegel, and everything that happened after him up to the moment when I decided to become a philosopher.
Philosophy in general, like every new philosophy, does not “fall from the sky.”
A new form of historical existence must therefore first come into being.
And that new existence is conditioned by everything that came before it.
World history as a whole is therefore the objective condition that makes this new philosophy possible.

The subjective condition—the condition that allows a particular individual to hope that he might be the philosopher who produces it—must obviously be knowledge of this history, insofar as history is the objective condition of the philosophy in question.
More precisely, the subjective condition is phenomenological knowledge of history.
A new philosophy becomes objectively possible when world history creates a new historical stage.

But subjectively—that is, for me—it becomes possible only when this stage begins to “exist for me”: when I become conscious of it and understand it, rather than merely participating in it “physically.”
Only then does an objective historical stage become a subjective stage as well.

The phenomenological description of the dialectical historical process that created the objective conditions making a new philosophy possible is therefore the necessary subjective condition that allows the author of that description to hope that he can turn this objective possibility into reality.

He does so by actually creating a new philosophy which, once embodied in a real book, separates itself, so to speak, from its author and becomes a real, objective part of the new historical period—at least if that period “recognizes” the book.
In this sense, the Phenomenology really is my philosophical autobiography.

It describes my philosophy through my own “activity”—through the philosophical formation or education I must undergo in order to become a philosopher, or at least to acquire the subjective possibility of becoming one.
And if this formation could—or can—turn me into a philosopher, then in principle it can do the same for anyone else who undergoes it: every reader who genuinely understands my Phenomenology.
We can therefore say that, by being a dialectical anthropology, the Phenomenology necessarily becomes a philosophical autobiography.
And by becoming a philosophical autobiography, it also serves as an Introduction to Philosophy.

It “introduces” both its author and its reader to philosophy because, by bringing them to full consciousness, it creates the subjective possibility for the author to produce the content of the complete self-consciousness called philosophy, and for the reader to reproduce that content—that is, to understand the philosophy.

And in doing so, Phenomenology guarantees to both author and reader the truth of that philosophy by showing its historical, dialectical necessity—and therefore its claim to universal, objective recognition.

We can stop here with our preliminary definition of the object and subject matter of Phenomenology. But one further point is worth noting. The idea of a “philosophical autobiography” that serves as an “introduction to Philosophy” is as old as philosophy itself.

We find it at the very beginning of Philosophy, in Plato’s “Socratic” Dialogues. Plato is not, of course, talking about himself but about Socrates. Yet since Plato presents Socrates, rather than himself, as the philosopher, we can say that the philosophical biography of Socrates contained in the Dialogues is effectively the philosopher’s autobiography. By showing how Socrates came to philosophy, it also helps anyone who understands the Dialogues to reach philosophy themselves. And these Dialogues must also establish the truth—that is, the necessity and universality—of the philosophy Plato sets out in his “Dogmatics,” namely his lost book On the Good.

The same thing happens at the beginning of Christian, medieval, theological philosophy. It begins with Augustine’s Confessions, which describe how and why Augustine arrived at Christianity. By showing the necessity of this “conversion,” the book is also meant to lead its readers to the same destination.

Then, at the dawn of “modern” philosophy, Descartes writes the Discourse on Method and the Meditations, and plans to write The History of My Mind. These works are all philosophical autobiographies: accounts of a path already travelled. By describing the path that led him to his philosophy, Descartes tries to establish the validity of that path by showing that it is necessary and universal. In other words, he tries to show that his autobiography is true while also making it accessible and understandable to everyone.

But only Hegel fully understood and explained why a philosophical autobiography is a necessary introduction to philosophy and a guarantee of its truth. In his Phenomenology, he showed what form such an autobiography must take if it is to achieve this goal.
